cards.back: Vector of first partial derivatives; it points toward steepest local increase for a differentiable scalar field.
The local rate of change of a scalar field along a specified unit direction.
A scalar relating objective and constraint gradients at a regular constrained optimum.
Matrix of second partial derivatives used to assess local curvature.
The local area or volume scaling factor introduced by a coordinate transformation.
A quantity per unit volume that is integrated over a region to obtain a total.
A scalar measure of local source or sink strength of a vector field.
A surface integral of the field component normal to an oriented boundary.
∇C = (∂C/∂x, ∂C/∂y) points toward steepest increase; |∇C| is that rate.
D_uC = ∇C · u for a unit vector u; zero along contour lines.
J = −D∇C: flux points down the gradient.
Fractional difference across a cell ≈ |∇C|L/C; absolute concentration also matters.
D = f_xx f_yy − f_xy²: D > 0 and f_xx > 0 minimum; D > 0 and f_xx < 0 maximum; D < 0 saddle.
At a constrained optimum ∇f = λ∇g; λ is the sensitivity of the optimum to the constraint.
h = 2r; open-topped: h = r.
dA = r dr dθ; the factor r is the Jacobian and often makes the integral solvable.
In an orthonormal frame, dot products measure projections; cross products encode oriented parallelogram area.
Integrate |r′| over the stated parameter range; repeated traversals count repeatedly.
Unit tangents and unit normals are dimensionless directions. Zero vectors cannot be normalized.
Components depend on frame; coordinate scales must be consistent before Euclidean norms are interpreted.
Change one variable with the others fixed. Existing coordinate partials alone do not guarantee differentiability.
df/dt=∇f·r′ for a static field; add explicit f_t when the field also evolves in time.
Differentiability supplies a linear approximation with remainder small relative to displacement length.
A Hessian norm bound M throughout the connecting segment gives linearization error at most M|h|²/2.
At a stationary point, positive determinant and positive leading entry give a minimum; negative determinant gives a saddle; zero is inconclusive.
Lagrange conditions require a regular constraint and yield candidates, not an automatic global guarantee.
Discard infeasible stationary points and compare every relevant edge and corner.
A multiplier's numerical sensitivity depends on the exact constraint scaling and sign convention.
Describe slices of the actual region before integrating; reconstruct bounds when reversing order.
Unsigned area or volume uses the absolute determinant, with the transformation domain and multiplicity checked.
Polar and cylindrical measure include r; spherical measure includes ρ²sinφ for the stated polar-angle convention.
Divide total by region measure; for a bounded nonnegative density, the average lies between its extrema.
Scalar accumulation uses C ds; oriented work uses F·dr. Reversal affects their signs differently.
For F=∇φ, line work is endpoint potential difference along admissible paths.
Counterclockwise outer boundary circulation equals the region integral of Q_x−P_y under the required smoothness.
Zero local curl does not prove global path independence on a punctured domain; all region boundaries and field conditions matter.
n dA equals the oriented parameter cross product; choose one convention and avoid double-counting area.
Net outward transfer over the full closed boundary equals the volume integral of divergence under its smoothness conditions.
Negative outward transfer is net inward supply; flux density and total transfer have different units.
Divergence of −D∇C includes ∇D terms when D varies; −D∇²C alone requires constant scalar D.
Choose the spanning-surface normal and boundary direction with the right-hand rule; circulation equals curl flux.
Storage change = integrated source minus sink minus net outward transfer for a fixed volume.
With no source or storage change, outward transfer equals minus integrated consumption.
Check the whole field region for singularities. Excluding an interior singularity can add a necessary inner boundary.
Multiply signed outward-normal density by area, then sum the whole boundary. Negative net outward transfer means inward supply.
For a smooth field and closed outward boundary, net transfer equals the integral of divergence over the enclosed volume.
A sink inferred from boundary transfer requires source and storage assumptions; steady, zero-source balance gives Q_out=−rV.
A common normal-density offset contributes offset times total boundary area; averaging repeats does not remove it.
For a positively oriented planar boundary C=∂D, Green’s circulation form relates ∮C F·dr to ∬D(∂Q/∂x−∂P/∂y)dA.
Choose the surface normal, then orient its boundary by the right-hand rule. Reversing orientation reverses the signed circulation.
Outward flux across the entire closed boundary of a solid equals the volume integral of divergence. An open surface patch alone is not that boundary.
Minimize D = Σ[yᵢ − (axᵢ + b)]²: aΣx² + bΣx = Σxy and aΣx + bn = Σy. Residuals of a fit with an intercept sum to zero.
D has constant Hessian [[2Σx², 2Σx], [2Σx, 2n]] with determinant 4[nΣx² − (Σx)²] > 0 when the x values are not all equal.
Fitting ln y = ln c + kx by a line minimizes errors in ln y, not y; a direct fit of y gives different c and k.
With a constraint, (∂w/∂x)_y and (∂w/∂x)_z differ. Use dw and the constraint differential, setting the held variable's differential to zero. Triple product: (∂x/∂y)_z(∂y/∂z)_x(∂z/∂x)_y = −1.
In polar coordinates dA = r dr dθ; the factor r is the Jacobian of (r, θ) ↦ (r cos θ, r sin θ).
The outward boundary integral ∮ J·n ds equals ∬ ∇·J dA when J is smooth on the closed region and the boundary is oriented with its outward normal.
With J = −D∇c, flux points down the gradient of c and scales with D; doubling D doubles every flux and every transfer.

cards.front: Which condition supports this selected implicit graph?
cards.back: A nonzero partial in the solved-for coordinate supplies a locally unique differentiable branch through the chosen point;it is not a global uniqueness claim.

cards.front: What is missing from a pointwise Hessian when certifying a Taylor remainder?
cards.back: A valid norm bound throughout the relevant segment or neighborhood,not merely one evaluated matrix.

cards.front: Which independent check verifies a graph path derivative?
cards.back: Differentiate the original constraint along the full spatial path and verify tangency with its gradient.

cards.front: Why separate a defining equation from its geometric set?
cards.back: A theorem’s sufficient nonvanishing condition can fail even when another chart or defining equation describes a regular object;actual branch geometry determines stronger claims.

cards.front: What does a Jacobian determinant supply?
cards.back: Local signed measure change;global inverse,transformed bounds and coverage need their own domain argument.

cards.front: Why can positive local orientation coexist with overcounting?
cards.back: Different distant input points can have the same image even when every local derivative is invertible and orientation preserving.

cards.front: Which checks can fail to detect repeated coverage?
cards.back: A total divided by a similarly overcounted area can still give the correct average;derive the map’s preimages or a once-covering domain independently.

cards.front: What must accompany a coordinate-change integral?
cards.back: Transformed bounds,the correct unsigned or oriented measure and a justified preimage/coverage description.

cards.front: What must be checked before identifying two iterated integrals?
cards.back: Their theorem’s integrability and domain conditions;executing both integrations symbolically does not establish those conditions.

cards.front: Why distinguish quadrature refinement from changing the cutoff?
cards.back: One improves a calculation on a fixed domain;the other changes the limiting problem and can intentionally change its value.

cards.front: What does the quarter-annulus calculation establish?
cards.back: A diverging absolute integral on a subregion,which rules out the missing finite absolute-integrability hypothesis on the full square.

cards.front: How should a regularized value be reported?
cards.back: With its exclusion or parameter rule and limiting convention,without relabeling it as a unique ordinary integral whose hypotheses fail.

cards.front: Why retain unrounded intermediates for a small finite-change error?
cards.back: Subtracting rounded values can overwhelm the small difference;the approximation error belongs to the exact supplied quantities,not the display precision.

cards.front: What can an interior multiplier calculation miss?
cards.back: Boundary extrema and multiple global maximizers;the complete feasible region and candidate comparison determine the global result.

cards.front: What establishes a usable one-to-one coordinate description?
cards.back: Explicit inverse or equivalent domain/preimage reasoning,together with transformed bounds and the local measure factor.

cards.front: How should a new nonlinear map be checked?
cards.back: Derive its actual Jacobian,radial/angular image and preimage count,then compare direct target integration with a justified once-covering pullback.

cards.front: What makes a divergence-theorem flux complete?
cards.back: Every outward boundary piece with the actual field,orientation and region,checked against the corresponding volume divergence under its smoothness hypotheses.

cards.front: Why keep scalar area separate from an oriented area vector?
cards.back: A unit normal times scalar dS and a parameter cross product are equivalent consistent flux conventions;combining both weights again double-counts surface measure.

cards.front: What must be stated when a singular expression has a cutoff-dependent value?
cards.back: The domain,order or exclusion path and limiting rule,with the failed ordinary-integrability condition distinguished from numerical error.

cards.front: Which global information does local curl omit?
cards.back: The field domain,the admissible spanning surface,boundary orientation and coverage counts;they are part of the theorem’s applicability.
a = (d|v|/dt)T + κ|v|²N. a_T = d|v|/dt = a·v/|v| changes the speed; a_N = κ|v|² = √(|a|² − a_T²) ≥ 0 turns the direction. Constant speed gives a ⟂ v.
κ = |T′|/|v| = a_N/|v|² = |v × a|/|v|³; the radius of curvature is 1/κ. It belongs to the path, not to the speed. A circle has κ = 1/R and a_N = v²/R; a line has κ = 0.

cards.front: Arc length without a closed form
cards.back: s = ∫|v|dt. When |v| has no elementary antiderivative, as for an ellipse, integrate numerically and check against bounds such as the inscribed and circumscribed circles.
d/dt(r × v) = r × a. If a is parallel to r, then r × v is constant and the areal speed ½|r × v| is constant (Kepler's second law), with r measured from the center of the acceleration.
M = ∬ δ dA; x̄ = (∬ xδ dA)/M, ȳ = (∬ yδ dA)/M. The center of mass lies within the body's extent, shifts toward denser regions and lies on any line of symmetry.
f̄ = (1/A)∬ f dA. It lies between the least and greatest values of f on the region, and M = δ̄A.
I = ∬ d²δ dA. About the z-axis d² = x² + y² = r², and the polar Jacobian r still multiplies. Uniform disk ½MR²; ring MR²; δ = kr gives 0.6MR²; rectangle M(a² + b²)/12.

I = I_cm + Md², where one axis passes through the center of mass and d is the distance between parallel axes. I_cm is the smallest. Density varying only along a cylinder's axis leaves I about that axis at ½MR².
